newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU's beef package prepares for further cuts.
newsitem.headline: EU's beef package prepares for further cuts.

text.p: Agreement to give the European Union's beef farmers more aid and cut production has paved the way for long-term reforms next year to cut output in line with sharply lower sales caused by mad cow disease, EU officials say.
European Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler says the package of mainly short-term measures and income aid will make negotiations in 1997 on the reforms easier.

But Germany disagrees, saying it voted against the deal agreed by farm ministers in Luxembourg on Wednesday because it reduced the pressure for the far-reaching changes needed to get rid of surpluses and bring the market back into balance.
The Commission is due to put forward proposals by April 1997 which will take account of a planned reform of the milk sector.
"The package (agreed on Wednesday) met the main objective of cutting surplus supplies linked to an 11 percent drop in demand," Fischler said after the three-day meeting.

It also provided 500 million Ecus ($635 million) extra aid for farmers hurt by the scare over bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), with French, German and British farmers receiving over half the total.
The money must be found from savings within the EU's 41- billion-Ecu ($51.25 billion) agricultural budget.

German Farm Minister Jochen Borchert said several measures in the 13-point package would only have a medium term impact on reducing beef production and should have been dealt with separately at a later date.
These included incentives to encourage less intensive livestock production from grass-fed herds and a reduction in national quotas of male cattle eligible for EU subsidies.
Germany was the only member state to reject the deal even though the EU's executive Commission and the EU's Irish presidency bent over backwards to try to meet German demands.

The final hour was spent trying to meet German objections to a single subsidy payment for bulls at 10 months of age, instead of two payments at 10 and 22 months, which Bonn said would drive many northern German farmers out of business.
Britain was among countries pressing for further reforms.
"I am determined to press for long term changes which benefit the agriculture industry," British farm minister Douglas Hogg said.
The mad cow crisis was triggered by a British government statement in March that the fatal cattle brain disease might be transmitted to people.
Demand for EU beef has since fallen by 11 percent and some 400,000 tonnes of unwanted beef have been put into storage.
Under Wednesday's agreement farm ministers agreed to buy up to 550,000 tonnes into public storage in 1996.
One of the main production-cutting measures was a German inspired scheme to slaughter one million calves which would reduce beef output by an estimated 300,000 tonnes in 1998.
Farm ministers asked their foreign affairs counterparts to review plans to increase imports of calves from eastern Europe to 500,000 animals a year, from 425,000.
Germans and Austrians especially see no logic in importing calves for fattening when the EU is trying to cut output.

But politically it would be difficult for the EU to withdraw the trade benefit granted under the so-called Europe agreements. Instead it might offer the east Europeans compensation if they agree not to export their cattle to the EU.
